The biodiesel industry established a voluntary quality assurance program known as BQ-9000 to support higher-quality fuels in the market. Under the RFS, biodiesel generally meets the biomass-based diesel 50% greenhouse gas emissions reduction threshold. This trend has continued through 2024 (EPA 2025d). 2.6.1 Production, Consumption, and Capacity Biodiesel is produced by transesterification—a process that converts fats and oils into biodiesel and glycerin (a coproduct) by reacting them with alcohol (typically methanol) and catalysts. Biodiesel production peaked at 1.8 billion gallons in 2018 and has declined in recent years to just under 1.7 billion gallons in 2024 (EIA 2025k). Excluding the 2 years of 2021 and 2022 when production nearly matched consumption, biodiesel consumption has generally exceeded production from 2015 to 2024 due to biodiesel imports (Figure 16). 2,200 2,000 1,800 1,600 1,400 1,200 1,000 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 Figure 16. Source: EIA (2025k) As of Jan. 1, 2025, there were 48 biodiesel plants with a total industry production capacity of nearly 2 billion gallons in 26 states (Figure 17 and Figure 18). Biodiesel plant capacity ranges from less than 1 million gallons to up to 144 million gallons. The average biodiesel plant size is about 42 million gallons. About 70% of the production comes from the Midwest; the largest biodiesel producer is Chevron Renewable Energy Group, which operates four plants with a total production capacity of 339 million annual gallons (EIA 2025o). Both the number of plants and capacity have declined since 2018; however, utilization of capacity has increased.
